headline_marked: [[Zero-shot models outperform XGBoost and LightGBM]] in new benchmarks on a laptop GPU
headline: Zero-shot models outperform XGBoost and LightGBM in new benchmarks on a laptop GPU
summary: Zero-shot models like Mitra v2 and TabPFN-3.5-Fast led primary metrics across three datasets, even running on a laptop GPU. Feature engineering still proved valuable for some foundation models.
details: A new benchmark compared zero-shot foundation models Mitra v2 and TabPFN-3.5-Fast against classical models XGBoost and LightGBM. The zero-shot models led each primary metric across three public datasets, demonstrating their performance potential.

The experiments used three UCI datasets (Online Shoppers, Seoul Bike, Dry Bean) with a 60% training, 20% validation, and 20% test split. Primary metrics were ROC-AUC, RMSE, and macro-F1, with all models using a fixed seed for consistency.

Mitra v2 with raw features achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.9366, surpassing LightGBM's 0.9321. TabPFN with engineered features led RMSE at 104.7439, significantly outperforming XGBoost's 179.4589. TabPFN also led macro-F1 with raw features at 0.9390.

While feature engineering did not improve ROC-AUC for foundation models on the Online Shoppers dataset, it substantially reduced RMSE for TabPFN and Mitra on the Seoul Bike dataset. Mitra's RMSE dropped from 205.1263 to 125.4689 with calendar features.

All 21 model variants were run on a laptop equipped with an NVIDIA RTX 3050 Laptop GPU (6 GB memory). Classical models ran on CPU, while foundation models utilized the GPU, confirming feasibility for local execution.

The benchmark suggests that zero-shot foundation models can indeed outperform traditional tree-based models on specific metrics and datasets. However, the study emphasizes that these results are based on single splits without significance tests, and further research is needed to establish universal superiority.

topic: moshcode deploys 50 ai agents for math proofs
headline_marked: [[moshcode work manages 50 AI agents]] with a single verifier and an inbox system
headline: moshcode work manages 50 AI agents with a single verifier and an inbox system
summary: The new moshcode 0.117.0 release introduces a robust workflow for managing numerous AI agents, drastically reducing human oversight by using a single, automated verifier. It streamlines the process of validating agent output and handling failures.
details: Traditionally, managing thousands of AI agents working on tasks like math proofs required extensive human oversight, often limited to what one person could monitor across multiple terminal panes. This approach capped effective management at around ten agents.

moshcode 0.117.0 introduces moshcode work, a new system designed to scale agent management. It employs headless worker processes, each in its own git worktree, with a mandatory verify command that dictates completion (exit 0).

The system ensures that failed attempts are re-queued with verification output for debugging, landing in an inbox after three failures for human review. Successful tasks incur minimal overhead, and atomic file renames allow several runs on a single queue.

The effectiveness was demonstrated by resolving 139 local test failures. The from-tests command identified one true failure, while the remaining 138 were PWA tests that crashed due to missing dependencies instead of skipping.

Fifty Claude workers processed 19 PWA tasks in parallel, with all passing on the first attempt, leaving the inbox empty and reducing local failures to zero. The single real failure, a mcp install test inheriting host PATH/HOME, was also successfully isolated and fixed.

Future enhancements will include verifiers beyond tests, such as typecheck errors, URL status checks, and integration with formal proof assistants like Lean. Users can upgrade via moshcode upgrade self.
